documented-feature-coverage.summary: `selka doc-coverage` fails the build when an implemented feature or a standard export has no documented example.

stable-incremental-identities.summary: Compiler identities for modules, declarations, bodies, types, specializations and emitted fragments are content-derived and stable across unrelated edits.

invalidation-report.summary: `selka check-project --explain-invalidation` reports per-stage hit/miss and the first changed dependency against a stored baseline; `--report` adds per-stage counts.

incremental-cache-contract.summary: Incremental cache keys include compiler identity, bootstrap version, target, runtime ABI, effects/capabilities contract and flags.

clean-warm-invalidation-matrix.summary: A clean-versus-warm invalidation matrix proves status, diagnostics, interface manifest and reuse counts agree.

list-interfaces-signature.summary: `selka list-interfaces` prints each exported callable's explicit signature, including capability parameter types, mut parameter markers and failure contracts.

capability-method-narrowing.summary: `fs.read_only()` returns a read-only `Filesystem` capability; it intersects permissions, performs no I/O, and contributes no effect.

filesystem-dir.summary: `fs.dir(path)` derives a `Filesystem` rooted at a literal path under the receiver's root; it is lazy, effect-free, and confines every acquisition to that subtree.

filesystem-dir-at.summary: `filesystem.dir_at(fs, path)` narrows a `Filesystem` to a folder named at run time: the path is read as `fs` reads one, the folder must be a directory reached without a symbolic link, and the result is the handle `fs.dir` gives, so narrowing only removes access.

environment-python-surface.summary: `env.get(name)` returns str? for any str name (a literal or a computed one; an empty name, one with NUL or `=`, or one over 255 octets answers None, and a name outside the allow-list or the `env.only` scope traps), `env.only(...)` narrows an Environment to literal names, and `env.names()` lists every visible name as str[].

failing-stand-in-capabilities.summary: `random.failing_entropy(after)` and `time.failing_clock(start, reads)` build an Entropy or Clock stand-in that answers a fixed number of reads normally and then fails every read as a provider that stopped working does, for fault-injection tests; they are deterministic and grant nothing.

filesystem-methods.summary: Every whole-path file helper also accepts a qualified method spelling on a `Filesystem` value (`fs.read_text(path)`), sharing the free form's arities, result types, literal-mode rule and trapping `with fs.open(...)` head; the method stays the receiver's even when a same-named function or local exists.

network-host.summary: `net.host(name)` narrows a `Network` to one literal endpoint; it is lazy, effect-free, and every acquisition through it requests exactly that endpoint.

network-python-surface.summary: The `network` standard module wraps `connect`, `read`, `write` and `close` over the raw network resource primitives.

network-endpoint-grant.summary: `selka run`, `run-project` and `build --run` accept repeatable `--allow-endpoint=IP:PORT` and `--allow-listen=IP:PORT` grants that provision a literal-only TCP provider for a `Network` entry point under `--restrict`; without a grant the entry point is refused.

network-server.summary: `network.listen(net)` binds a `Listener` through a narrowed endpoint and `accept_resource[Accepted](listener)` accepts one `Connection` while borrowing the listener; `--allow-listen=IP:PORT` grants only that literal local endpoint.

network-memory.summary: `network.memory()` is a deterministic `Network` stand-in whose `net.host(name)` endpoints live in memory: `listen`, `connect` and `accept_resource` make and hand out connected ends, bytes written on one end queue on the other, and a read, accept or connect that a real socket would wait for fails at once with the code 3. A name is held only while a live listener has it: a second `listen` on it is refused with the code 3 while the first listener is used later, and succeeds once the first has been used for the last time or its scope has ended.

network-event-loop.summary: `network.open_poller(net)` returns one `Poller` that owns a listener and up to 1,024 accepted connections named by integer ids; `wait`, `accept`, `recv`, `send` and `close_connection` never block beyond a timeout, report readable, writable, hangup, error and idle events, and add no compiler builtin.

network-listen-port-zero.summary: `--allow-listen=IP:0` lets a program bind a kernel-chosen port through `net.host("IP:0")` and a `Poller`, which reports the port with `network.port`.

network-run-time-addresses.summary: `network.connect_to`, `connect_within_to`, `listen_at`, `open_poller_at`, `dial_to` and `dial_within_to` take the address as a `str` at run time, checked when they run against `--allow-endpoint` and `--allow-listen` exactly as a `net.host` literal is (every address without `--restrict`); a narrowed Network refuses any other address with 2, `network.memory()` takes any text as a name, and `acquire_resource` on a Network is the standard library's own (`E_INTERNAL_NAME`).

network-connect-within.summary: `network.connect_within(net, network.Timeouts(connect_ms=, read_ms=, write_ms=))` connects like `connect` within time limits kept on the socket (no thread or signal): a connect, read or write that runs out fails with its own code `network.timed_out()` (7), distinct from a refused endpoint (3) and a closed peer, and a zero limit is none.

network-connection-idle-timeout.summary: `network.set_connection_idle_timeout(poller, id, millis, mut outcome)` gives one Poller connection its own idle timeout (0 never, negative back to the poller's), replacing `set_idle_timeout`'s value for it alone.

http-write-response-head.summary: `http.write_response_head(response)` writes the header section of the GET answer, its Content-Length included, and no body: the answer to a HEAD request.

http-parse-prefix.summary: `http.parse_request_prefix(data, limits)` and `http.parse_response_prefix(data, closed)` parse the one message at the start of `data` and answer, beside it, how many octets it took (`length`: the header section, its blank line and the body), so a server that keeps a connection open moves on to the next message; an incomplete message is still `Incomplete`.

http-strict-reading.summary: `http` reads a message strictly where two readers could disagree on its framing: Content-Length and a chunk size are digits only, a status code is exactly three digits, a control octet in a field value, reason or version is refused and never trimmed, a request target is one of the four forms of RFC 9112 (`*` and an authority form have no path), a trailer cannot name a framing field, and the writers check the method, the version and the framing and give an empty body `Content-Length: 0`.

http-request-limits.summary: `http.parse_request_within(data, http.Limits(header_bytes=, header_fields=, body_bytes=))` parses a request within the caller's limits, whose defaults are `parse_request`'s; a body past the limit is `BodyTooLarge` (413), never `Malformed`.

network-poller-dial.summary: `network.dial(mut poller, net, mut outcome)` and `dial_within(..., limits, ...)` open a connection from the event loop to the endpoint a narrowed Network names and name it by an id, as `accept` does; nothing blocks, `wait` reports `EVENT_CONNECTED` or `EVENT_ERROR` (refused, unreachable, past `connect_ms`), and the dial needs the grant a blocking `connect` needs.

network-client-poller.summary: `network.open_client_poller(net)` returns a `Poller` that listens on nothing, so a program that only connects out holds many connections in one without a listen grant: `dial`, `dial_to` and their `_within` forms add connections, each dial still needs its `--allow-endpoint`, `accept` answers `OUTCOME_WOULD_BLOCK`, and the limit is the descriptor limit less 64.

network-receive-buffer.summary: `network.Timeouts(receive_buffer_bytes=N)` sets a connection's receive buffer (`SO_RCVBUF`, before the connect) for `connect_within` and `dial_within`; 0, the default, keeps the system's.

hashes-sha1.summary: `hashes.sha1(data)` (40 hexadecimal digits) and `hashes.sha1_bytes(data)` (20 octets) give SHA-1 for protocols that require it, such as the WebSocket handshake; it is not for security.

host-capability-foreign-calls.summary: Every extern func takes host: Host as its first parameter; the checker requires that capability at each call and the C ABI drops it before the foreign call, with --allow-host under --restrict.

buffered-stream-write.summary: `write(out, buffer)` writes a mutable byte buffer's current octets straight out of its own storage, with no snapshot copy and the same `output` effect as a byte string.

stream-capability.summary: `print(out, ...)`/`print(err, ...)` and `write(out, text)` write through a `Stream` capability and contribute the `output` effect.

debug-line.summary: `debug(values...)` writes to standard error without a capability and contributes no effect; a `build --release` binary evaluates its arguments, in order, and drops only the formatting and the write.

error-conversion.summary: Prefix `try` converts a propagated error into the enclosing failure type when its enum has a case whose payload is that error type.

error-return-traces.summary: An error reaching main or a test is reported with its return trace: its construction or runtime call, every prefix try propagation and conversion, and each return that passed it on, retained in a bounded ring only on error paths.

standard-error-unions.summary: Fallible standard modules export error enums with named string payload fields and a message(error) helper, rather than returning unstructured string errors.

reference-command.summary: `selka reference --query TERM [--format=text|json]` answers from data embedded in the running executable: implemented features with their documentation anchors, supported boundaries, unsupported and removed names, embedded standard-library declarations with their signatures, analysis status and mutation facts, and the checker's own builtin and collection-method vocabulary.

agent-context.summary: `selka context <entry.selka> --symbol 'module::name'` or `--at 'path:line:column'` answers one `agent-context-v1` object about one declaration from the facts `selka index-project`, `selka list-interfaces`, `selka tests-for` and `selka api-diff` already publish: declaration, contract with fact status, types, dependencies, tests and optional changes in a fixed priority order inside a `--context-bytes` budget, with per-section `omissions`, a `continuation` query, and a labeled partial answer on an incomplete project.

keyword-only-parameters.summary: `named name: T` marks each parameter individually; calls supply its explicit label in any order, and callable types retain named labels as part of their contract.

test-file-private-access.summary: A module named `<name>_test` that no other module imports may call the private functions, types and constants of module `<name>`, so a helper need not become `public` to be tested; every other importer still gets `E_PRIVATE_SYMBOL`.

per-entry-cases-files.summary: `selka test ENTRY` without `--cases` applies the `<stem>.cases.json` beside the entry, so a directory run applies each entry's own cases file to that entry and a single-file run sees the same cases.

bytes-sorting.summary: Stable sorted and list.sort accept bytes elements and scalar or recursively ordered record keys containing bytes.

text-trim-charsets.summary: Text and bytes trim explicit character sets with Python defaults.

text-search-ranges.summary: Text and bytes search/count/prefix/suffix ranges and checked index lookup use nonnegative explicit positions; negative positions trap and upper range endpoints clamp.

scalar-repr.summary: Exact CPython scalar repr with Unicode16 printability and shortest float formatting.

memory-bounded-test-fanout.summary: A test run sizes its worker pool from free memory as well as cores (each per-test ceiling plus 256 MiB of headroom must fit in MemAvailable), with --jobs and SELKA_JOBS to override it.

function-digest.summary: Compiler-issued callable and reachable dependency identities bind source schemas and execution context; unavailable authority returns an empty string.

durable-storage.summary: Native filesystem capabilities provide bounded complete directory listings and regular-file reads, atomic synchronized writes, directory synchronization and crash-released exclusive directory leases.

filesystem-large-listings.summary: `listdir` and `list_directory` answer a directory of any size whole, on a real directory and on `filesystem.memory()`; the bound of `list_directory` is the caller's (any non-negative `max_entries`), and a directory over it, or a negative bound, is refused in words that name the bound rather than the grants.

standard-spans.summary: The `spans` module: a `Sources` table holds the text of every file a program reads for as long as the table lives, and a `Span` (file, start, length: three integers) names a piece of it, so long-lived data points into the source without a copy of the text; `text` is a borrowed view that traps `R_ASSERT` outside the table, and spans compare and hash by text in place.

standard-symbols.summary: The `symbols` module interns a name once and answers a `Symbol`, one integer that is copied, compared with `==` and used as a dictionary key; `find` looks a name up without adding it, `name` reads it back as a borrowed view, and `intern_span` interns the text a span names.

long-lived-keys.summary: Long-lived data holds a key, not a borrow: a span into a source table, a symbol for a repeated name, the key of a cache entry that the filling call answers and the caller reads in place; a cache is a table.

standard-byte-format.summary: The `byte_format` module: `shortest` and `decimal` append Zig's `{d}` and `{d:.N}` of a float to a byte builder (checked against the pinned Zig toolchain), and `format`, `format1`, `format2` and `format3` write a template whose `{d}`, `{d:.N}` and `{s}` placeholders take numbers and borrowed texts, so one call replaces the run of literal and number appends a Zig `w.print` becomes; a template that does not fit its arguments traps `R_ASSERT`.

filesystem-replace-file.summary: `replace_file(fs, path, data)` and `replace_file_mode(fs, path, data, mode)` publish a file atomically (a temporary beside the destination, renamed over it) without synchronizing it, as Zig's `AtomicFile` does; `atomic_write_file` keeps the synchronized, durable publication. A small write is well under a millisecond instead of about 40 ms on ext4, and the in-memory filesystem answers both.

filesystem-replace-file-synced.summary: `replace_file_synced(fs, path, data)` and `replace_file_synced_mode(fs, path, data, mode)` publish a file atomically (a temporary beside the destination, renamed over it) and force the file to disk before the rename but not the directory after it: one `fsync` where `atomic_write_file` makes two and `replace_file` none. After a power loss the old file or the complete new one is there; the rename may be lost. The mode rule, the refusals and the error text are `replace_file`'s, and the in-memory filesystem answers them too.

filesystem-list-entries.summary: `filesystem.list_entries(fs, path)` lists a directory with each entry's kind (`Regular`, `Directory`, `Symlink`, `Other`) taken from the directory record, so a walk needs no `stat` per entry; `filesystem.memory()` answers it too, sorted. `stat_path` is one `fstatat` from a descriptor the capability keeps open (an unrestricted root) or one confined `openat2` below a granted root, where it was three to thirteen system calls.

filesystem-rename-stat-lock.summary: Native filesystem capabilities add `rename_path` (atomic rename inside one granted directory, never a copy across devices), `stat_path` and the typed `filesystem.stat` (kind, size, modification time in nanoseconds and inode; a missing path is the matchable `StatError.Missing`) and the advisory exclusive `flock` file locks `lock_file` and `try_lock_file`, which are released when their `with` scope or the process ends. They honour `--allow-read`, `--allow-write` and `--restrict` like the other durable calls and are refused on the in-memory filesystem.

filesystem-real-paths.summary: Native filesystem capabilities add `canonical_path` and the typed `filesystem.realpath` and `filesystem.cwd` (the link-free absolute path with or without a restriction, the path relative to the narrowing on an `fs.dir` handle, refusing a result outside a grant), `chmod_path`, `touch_path` and `set_modified_path` (final component not followed), `atomic_write_file_mode` (publication with chosen permissions where `atomic_write_file` keeps 0600), `stat_follow_path` and `filesystem.stat_follow`, and `Stat.mode`; an unrestricted `stat` and `listdir` pass through symbolic links as `read_text` does. The in-memory filesystem answers them too.

filesystem-symlink.summary: `symlink_path(fs, target, path)` and `filesystem.symlink(fs, target, path)` create the symbolic link `path` holding the text `target`, stored as written, with the grant every other write has (write authority, a path inside the granted directory, a free name, an existing directory that holds no link). `realpath` and `stat_follow` follow a link only inside the granted directory and every other call refuses a link on the way or a read, write or lock of one, so a program can build the tree that tests of those refusals need; the in-memory filesystem keeps links as entries with the same rules and wording.

stat-changed.summary: `Stat.changed` is the status-change time (`ctime`) in nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, a sixth word of `stat_path`'s answer: the kernel moves it for any change to an entry, `set_modified` included, so a file rewritten and given its old modification time still shows a newer `changed`. A constructor may leave it out (it defaults to `0`); the in-memory filesystem gives it the write's logical clock reading, and a nanosecond past the last change for `chmod` and `set_modified`, which leave the clock where it is.

stat-device.summary: `Stat.device` is the `st_dev` the kernel names for an entry, the seventh word of `stat_path`'s answer (56 octets), so an inode can be named with its device as `/proc/locks` writes a lock's file (`MAJ:MIN:INODE`); `filesystem.device_major(device)` and `filesystem.device_minor(device)` take the number apart as `major(3)` and `minor(3)` do. A constructor may leave it out (`0`), and every entry of a `memory()` filesystem is on the one device `filesystem.MEMORY_DEVICE` (major 0, minor 1).

filesystem-statfs.summary: `filesystem.statfs(fs, path)` (the builtin `statfs_path`) answers a `filesystem.Space`, the `size_bytes`, `free_bytes` and `available_bytes` of the filesystem that holds `path`, as `statfs(2)` does with blocks times the fragment size; a missing path is `StatError.Missing`, any other refusal `Failed(message)`, under the grants `stat` needs (read authority, no `.` or `..` component, no link under `--restrict`). A `memory()` filesystem answers the fixed numbers 1073741824, 536870912 and 402653184.

filesystem-read-at.summary: `filesystem.read_at(fs, path, offset, max_bytes)` (the builtin `read_at_path`, with the offset packed as eight octets) answers at most `max_bytes` octets of a regular file from byte `offset` with `pread`: fewer at the end of the file and none past it, so a program that follows a file that only grows reads only what was appended. The file is opened as `read_regular_file` opens it, the count is bounded by 64 MiB, and a negative offset or count fails; the in-memory filesystem answers the same.

filesystem-read-link.summary: `filesystem.read_link(fs, path)` (the builtin `read_link_path`) answers the text stored in the symbolic link at `path`, as `readlink(2)` does and without following it: relative or absolute, dangling or not, the first link's text for a link to a link. It resolves its path as `stat` does on every kind of root (no restriction, a `--restrict` grant, an `fs.dir(...)` narrowing, `fs.read_only()` and the in-memory filesystem), so it refuses a link on the way and a `.` or `..` component as `stat` does, and reads a link whose target is outside the grant. Any other entry fails with `is not a symbolic link`.

filesystem-link.summary: `filesystem.link(fs, target, path)` (the builtin `link_path`, also `fs.link_path(target, path)`) creates the hard link `path` to the existing regular file `target`, as `link(2)` does: a second name for one file, sharing its bytes, permission bits, times and inode, so `Stat.links` reads 2 for both until one is removed. Each of the two paths is resolved as `symlink` resolves its own (a plain run as a process reads a path; `--restrict` both inside write grants, so a file that can only be read is never linked into a place that can be written; a narrowed `fs.dir` handle both inside its folder; `fs.read_only()` refuses), with no link followed on the way or at the end of `target`; `target` must be a regular file (a folder fails with `is a directory`, a symbolic link with the link wording, anything else with `is not a regular file`). A failure reads `link 'TARGET' to 'PATH': REASON`. A `memory()` filesystem keeps one shared file for the names (bytes, mode, times, lock), and the permission matrix pins its refusals to the real directory's.

filesystem-mkdir-mode.summary: `filesystem.mkdir_mode(fs, path, mode)` (the builtin `mkdir_mode`, also `fs.mkdir_mode(path, mode)`) creates the folder `path` with the permission bits `mode` (`0` to `0o7777`) as `mkdir(2)` takes them, so the folder never exists with the default mode, which `fs.mkdir` then `chmod` leaves it with until the `chmod` runs. The umask narrows `mode` as it narrows a file's (`atomic_write_file_mode`); the system keeps the nine permission bits and the sticky bit and leaves the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits to `chmod`. The path is resolved as the durable calls resolve one (a trailing slash names the folder to make) and fails with `already exists` or `the parent directory does not exist`, with `mkdir 'PATH': REASON`; the same grants as `link` decide where it may write. A `memory()` filesystem stores the mode as given.

filesystem-create-mode.summary: `filesystem.create_mode(fs, path, mode) -> File fails str` (the builtin `create_mode`, also `fs.create_mode(path, mode)`, which a `with` may open directly) opens `path` for writing as `fs.open(path, "wb")` does, and a file it creates gets the permission bits `mode` (`0` to `0o7777`) in the one `open(2)` that makes it, as `creat(2)` takes them, so a member recorded `0o600` is never readable by the group while it fills, which `fs.open` then `chmod` leaves it. The umask narrows `mode`. A file that exists is truncated and keeps its own mode, as `fs.open(path, "wb")` leaves it. The path rule is that of every write (a write grant under `--restrict`, a narrowed handle's folder, no link followed but by the unrestricted handle); failures read `open 'PATH': REASON`. A `memory()` filesystem stores the mode as given.

stat-owner-group-links.summary: `Stat.owner`, `Stat.group` and `Stat.links` are the `st_uid`, `st_gid` and `st_nlink` of an entry, the eighth to tenth words of `stat_path`'s answer (80 octets), for `stat` and `stat_follow`. A constructor may leave them out (`0`); every entry of a `memory()` filesystem is owned by `filesystem.MEMORY_OWNER` and `filesystem.MEMORY_GROUP` (1000), a file or a link has one link and a directory two plus the directories inside it.

filesystem-memory-permissions.summary: The in-memory filesystem honours the permission bits it keeps, as an ordinary user who owns every entry: the owner bits decide, a write without the write bit of a file, a creation, removal or rename without the write bit of its directory, a read without the read bit and a path through a directory without the search bit fail with the real provider's words (`permission denied`; `permission denied` for `write_file` of a new file as for every other call). A read-only file in a writable directory is still replaced by a publication, as on disk. The calls and bits are tabulated in the documentation, and one program of about 490 calls is pinned against a real directory.

filesystem-memory-durable.summary: `filesystem.memory()`, which is also a test's `fs`, answers the whole durable family from its own entries: atomic writes, rename (files and directories), `stat` with a mode, an inode and a time from a logical clock that starts at the test clock's epoch and moves one second per changing call, `chmod`, `touch`, `set_modified`, `realpath`, bounded reads, sorted listings and the three locks, which are released on every exit of their `with` scope. `try_lock_file` and a second `lock_directory` on a held path fail with the busy text; `lock_file` fails at once because a stand-in cannot wait. Deterministic, so tests that use it stay cached.

standard-hashes.summary: `hashes.sha256(data)` returns the SHA-256 digest of a `bytes` value as 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, and `data.sha256()` or `text.sha256()` answers the 32 raw octets as `bytes`. The C runtime hashes the octets in place, with the x86 SHA extensions when the CPU has them (chosen at run time) and portable C otherwise, both giving the same digest.

standard-input.summary: An `Input` entry parameter (any name) is the process's standard input, granted unconditionally like `Stream` (`--restrict` cannot remove it). `stdin.read(max)` answers up to `max` octets (empty at the end), `stdin.read_exact(n)` exactly `n` or `None` when the input ends first, `stdin.read_line()` a line with its newline, the final unterminated line or `None`, and `stdin.read_into(mut buffer, max)` appends one read to a `byte_buffer` and counts it. A refused read or a negative size traps `R_INPUT`. `streams.input_from(bytes)` builds an in-memory input for tests, and a test function that declares an `Input` parameter is given an empty one.

registers-capability.summary: A `Registers` capability and the `registers` module read and write hardware registers (`read8`, `read16`, `read32`, `write8`, `write16`, `write32`). On Linux `main` cannot ask for one (`E_MAIN`); `registers.simulated()` makes a simulated bank, one little-endian memory of bytes with a log of every write (`write_count`, `writes`, `last_write`) and `poke32` to set what a read answers, so driver code is tested with no board. The bank is allocated whole, so reads and writes are legal in a `@noalloc` function; a full bank traps `R_REGISTER_BANK`. It is a shareable handle, refused as a task argument and as text.

cpu-builtins.summary: The `cpu` module: `wait_for_event`, `wait_for_interrupt`, `send_event`, `barrier` (`dsb sy` then `isb sy`), `breakpoint`, and `interrupts_off` with `interrupts_restore`, each taking `Registers`. `interrupts_off` answers a sealed `@linear` `InterruptState`, so a path that forgets the restore does not compile. On a device each is the instruction itself as inline assembly; on a simulated bank each is recorded in an event log (`event_count`, `events`, `count_of`, `interrupts_are_off`, `write_with_interrupts_off`) that a device build refuses.

stop-capability.summary: A `Stop` entry parameter lets a program hear that it is being stopped: SIGTERM and SIGINT turn `process.stop_requested(stop)` true instead of ending it, the next `network.wait` of each poller and the next real `time.sleep` end early, and a second signal ends the program by the default action. A program without a `Stop` has no handler and dies as before. It needs no grant (`--restrict` keeps it), is a shareable handle like `Stream`, is refused as a task argument, and a test gets a stand-in (`process.simulated_stop()`, triggered by `process.request_stop`).

process-capability.summary: A `Process` entry parameter grants the right to start programs: `selka run` and installed executables grant it, `--restrict` needs `--allow-process` (or `--allow-all`) and otherwise refuses to start with the usual withheld-capability line. `process.run(proc, request)` runs a program (no shell: an argument list, optional working directory, standard input and explicit environment) to completion and answers its exit status or terminating signal with its standard output and standard error captured up to a limit; a missing program is the matchable `Error.NotFound`.

process-start.summary: `process.start(proc, request, stdout_path, stderr_path)` starts a program without waiting (standard input /dev/null, output to the named files or /dev/null) and returns a sealed `@linear` `process.Child` that only `start` makes and that ends exactly once, by `process.wait` or `process.stop` (SIGTERM, a grace, SIGKILL); `process.signal` reaches only a started program no wait has reaped, `process.wait_within(proc, mut child, millis)` answers its `Output` or None while it runs, a started program is killed when the Selka program ends first, and a scripted Process answers `start` from its rules with a Child that has already ended. Every child (`run` and `start`) gets the address-space limit the Selka program started with, not its memory ceiling.

process-start-to.summary: `process.start_to(proc, request, stdout, stderr)` is `process.start` with a `process.Destination` for each output stream: `Discard` (/dev/null), `File(path)` or `Caller`, which lets the started program write straight to the caller's own standard output or standard error while it runs, as a shell does by default (what the caller printed so far is flushed first). It grants nothing the caller lacks, so `--restrict` changes nothing about it; a test's scripted Process starts nothing and ignores the destinations.

process-group.summary: `process.group()` makes a sealed `@linear` `process.Group` that holds any number of started programs, which a `Child` cannot be kept in: `group_start` and `group_start_to` start a program into it as `start` and `start_to` do (no new capability) and answer its key (0, 1, 2, ...), each program leading a process group of its own; `group_wait_any_within(proc, mut g, millis)` and `group_wait_any` answer the key and the exit status or signal of the first program to end (a program that ended unseen is not lost; the wait polls every program's pidfd, so it sleeps until one ends); `group_signal` and `group_signal_all` reach each program and what it started; `group_stop` sends SIGTERM, waits a grace and sends SIGKILL to every process group; `group_size` and `group_pid` read the group; `group_close(proc, own g, grace)` stops the programs still running and ends the group. A scripted Process answers a group's starts from its rules, the programs already ended.

process-scripted.summary: A test's `proc: Process` parameter and `process.scripted(rules)` are scripted Processes that start nothing: `process.run` logs the request and answers from the first rule (`Rule`: program, an argument prefix, a `Reply` of an exit, a missing program or a refusal, and a use count) that covers it, or fails `scripted Process has no rule for [argv]`; `process.expect(proc, rule)` adds a rule and `process.calls(proc)` reads the log. A test needs no grant and stays cacheable, because the script is program text. `process.executable_path(proc)` answers the running program's absolute path (a scripted Process answers `process.SCRIPTED_EXECUTABLE_PATH`).

standard-binary-codec.summary: The `binary` module writes little-endian fixed-width integers, LEB128 varints (zigzag for signed) and length-prefixed bytes and text to a `byte_builder.Builder`, and reads them back from `bytes` with a caller-held position; a read that cannot finish fails with `Truncated`, `Overlong` or `Text` and leaves the position unchanged, `get_length` reads a field's size without copying it, and `bytes.read_u8` is the inline single-octet read. A byte-buffer octet append stores in line when the block has room.

standard-blake3.summary: `hashes.blake3(data)` and `hashes.blake3_text(text)` return the 32-byte BLAKE3 digest as a `hashes.Digest`, a record of four `u64` words that compares with `==`, keys a dictionary and prints through `hashes.hex`; `hashes.to_bytes`, `hashes.from_bytes` and `hashes.from_hex` convert it, and `data.blake3()` answers the 32 raw octets. The hash runs in the prebuilt Zig runtime over the octets in place, within the 1.10x parity rule of Zig's `std.crypto.hash.Blake3`.

standard-cache-record.summary: Canonical string-array records carry an exact version and SHA-256 checksum; malformed or noncanonical records are rejected.

standard-persistent-memo.summary: Bounded persistent byte snapshots use exact tagged inputs and compiler-issued callable identity, verified records and exclusive atomic publication.

standard-durable.summary: Pure chunk/state pipelines retain verified committed progress and recover final file publication after a process crash.

field-requirements.summary: A generic parameter may require named fields in addition to built-in bounds. Field requirements preserve nominal identity and are checked in unused generic bodies and forwarding calls.

explicit-capability-arguments.summary: Authority is an explicit capability argument such as Filesystem, Network, Stream or Host. Calling an operation requires its capability value; source effect ceilings and inferred effect summaries are absent.

guest-callbacks.summary: Guest callback signatures retain parameter types, named labels, mut positions and failure contracts. Named functions supply callbacks; context is an explicit argument, without inferred effect ceilings or captured environments.

freestanding-functions.summary: @freestanding marks a function that needs nothing from the runtime: unmanaged data only, calls only of other @freestanding functions, extern funcs and inline built-ins (the registers reads and writes), and an assert with no message. The check refuses a broken rule with E_FREESTANDING; a failed check inside one is a fault that calls nothing (its code and place in registers, then the trap instruction), and the emitted code is verified to name no runtime symbol.

noalloc-attribute.summary: @noalloc requires ownership-expanded Core allocation analysis at build/run/test to prove that the function does not allocate. Violations report E_NOALLOC_ALLOCATES and fail before execution; plain check does not compute this Core contract.

python-print.summary: print(out, ...) renders values Python-style through an explicit Stream argument.

text-scalar-helpers.summary: `str` is bytes: `len` is the octet count, `text[i]` is one octet as an `int`, and `text[a:b]` is a byte-offset copy that traps R_TEXT_BOUNDARY when an endpoint falls inside a scalar. `strings.char_count`, `char_at`, `char_slice`, `char_stride`, `chars` and `bytes` are the scalar reading, and `lists.stride` is the stepped list copy; iterating a `str` directly and stepped slices are refused with their certain fix.

text-byte-semantics.summary: `len(text)`, `text[i]` and `text[a:b]` read octets, and a byte-offset slice endpoint inside a multi-byte scalar traps `R_TEXT_BOUNDARY`. Text search positions stay scalar, so they compose with the `strings.char_*` helpers.

needless-copy-warning.summary: A `copy(value)` whose copy-free form checks is the checker warning `W_NEEDLESS_COPY`, with the certain `fix` that deletes the call or writes the move (`own`, `take`, a consuming loop); `selka lint` reports it as `L_NEEDLESS_COPY`, blocks under `--gate`, and a copy that is the point of the code takes a reasoned waiver. Where the move needs a rewrite the checker cannot make, `W_COPY_MOVE` names the form and `L_COPY_MOVE` reports it.

copy-in-recursion-warning.summary: A `copy(...)` of a function's context (a parameter, a loop variable over one, or a place of either) inside a record passed to the function's own recursive call is the warning `W_COPY_IN_RECURSION`, which names the borrowed form; where every field then borrows, its `fix` deletes the record's copies together.

loop-linear-search.summary: `L_LINEAR_SEARCH_IN_LOOP` names a list a loop appends to and searches in the same loop, and its rewrite is a `set` or `dict` kept alongside; it reports everywhere and refuses only in a declaration changed against `--against REF`. A search on a list the loop does not change only reports.

loop-shift.summary: `L_SHIFT_IN_LOOP` names a list declared outside a loop that removes or inserts at index 0 inside it, and its rewrite is an index cursor or B6's `deque`; it reports everywhere and refuses only in a declaration changed against `--against REF`.

loop-sort.summary: `L_SORT_IN_LOOP` names a list a loop appends to and sorts in the same loop, and its rewrite is one sort after the loop or B6's `heap`; it reports everywhere and refuses only in a declaration changed against `--against REF`. A list built inside the iteration and sorted once there does not fire.

loop-copy.summary: `L_COPY_IN_LOOP` reads the `cost --sites` rows: a copy the Core passes at loop depth 1 or more is reported in every declaration, names the rewrites in order (a field store, `exchange`, a borrowing `const`, an `own` hand-off), and refuses under `--gate` only in a declaration changed against `--against REF`. A reasoned waiver takes a copy that is the point.

loop-alloc.summary: `L_ALLOC_IN_LOOP` reads the `cost --sites` rows: a construction or conversion site at loop depth 1 or more names its kind and that kind's hint, reports only in a declaration changed against `--against REF`, and never refuses. It reuses the build's own allocation classification, so the lint finding and `selka cost --sites` cannot disagree.

testing-work-growth.summary: The `testing` standard module states a workload's growth class instead of timing it: `testing.steps(work, n)` is the executed blocks, `testing.allocations(work, n)` and `testing.allocations_writing(work, out, n)` are the managed blocks the runtime allocated (the event `--counters` reports as `allocs`), and `testing.growth(work, small, large)` is the larger of the two counts' growth ratios. `testing.linear` fails when either count grows by more than 1.5x the step from `small` to `large` (6x at 1,000 to 4,000), `testing.constant` allows 1.5x plus two counts of slack, a count zero at both sizes passes, and a failure names the counter, both values and the ratio.

performance-idiom-growth-suite.summary: `tests/lang/performance_idioms.selka` gates the B0 idiom shapes as growth tests in optimized debug and release: each fixed idiom asserts its class through `testing.linear` or `testing.constant`, each quadratic idiom asserts through `testing.growth` that `linear` would fail, storing an f-string allocates once per string and printing one allocates nothing. The managed-allocation counter is off around ordinary tests and enabled only while a measurement runs; the counter readers are reserved to `testing` and trap `R_NO_STEP_ACCOUNTING` in a program that carries no executed-block accounting.

byte-reads.summary: `bytes.read_u16_be`, `bytes.read_u32_le` and their siblings read one fixed-width integer or float at an offset of `bytes`, a view or a slice, with one bounds check for the whole width; an offset outside the value traps `R_LIST_BOUNDS`.

take-and-exchange.summary: `take(mut place)` moves a value out of a writable local, record field, list element (`xs[i]`, `xs[i].f`) or `match mut` binding and leaves its type's default value (an empty collection, None for an optional, or a record built from its field defaults); `exchange(mut place, value)` moves the old value of any type but a resource out and puts the replacement in, a named replacement taking `own`. Both answer the moved value, owned, with no copy, and work in generic bodies. Dictionary values, unmarked or borrowed places, and `take` of a type with no default are refused.

detach-loops.summary: `for x in detach r.items:` moves a list out of a record's field (or a list element's field) for the loop, so the body may change the record with `mut`, and puts it back at every exit: running out, `break`, `return`, `fail` and a failing `try`, with no copy. Inside the loop the place is empty; a `return` or `fail` value is computed before the put-back, and one that borrows the loop variable is refused. A place written while set aside traps `R_ASSERT`; a dictionary value, a call and two names are refused (`E_ITERATION`).

consuming-loops.summary: `for x in own xs:` takes the list an owned local or `own` parameter holds and gives each element to `x` as its owner, in order and with no copy; an element the body does not move is dropped at the end of its iteration, an early `break`, `return` or `fail` drops the rest, and `xs` is moved from the loop on. A `mut` or borrowed list, a field, a call result and two names are refused (`E_ITERATION`).

float-zig-exact-log-exp-atan2-pow.summary: `math.log10`, `exp`, `atan2` and `pow_float`, and their `f32_` forms, answer the bits of Zig's `std.math.log10`, `exp`, `atan2` and `pow`, special values included.

float-zig-exact-ln-trig-hyperbolic.summary: `math.ln`, `atan`, `acos`, `asin`, `tan`, `expm1`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `cbrt`, `sin` and `cos` answer the bits of Zig's `@log`, `std.math.atan`, `acos`, `asin`, `@tan`, `std.math.expm1`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `cbrt`, `@sin` and `@cos`, with the Payne-Hanek reduction so no finite argument traps.

list-concatenation.summary: `left + right` on two lists of one element type is a new list holding copies of the elements of both, left first; neither operand changes and a managed element is copied.

bytes-replace.summary: `bytes.replace(data, old, new)` replaces every non-overlapping occurrence of `old` in a byte string, as `strings.replace` does for `str`; an empty `old` traps with `R_EMPTY_SEPARATOR`.

capability-records.summary: A function that takes capabilities as `own` parameters builds and returns a record that holds them; the caller binds it, passes it `mut`, and forwards named capabilities with `own`.

check-directory.summary: `selka check DIR` checks every module of the project beneath DIR, imported or not, through one generated entry.

local-path-root-precedence.summary: A local, parameter, `for` variable, `with` name or `match` payload named like the root of an imported dotted path (`eval` beside `import eval.deprecations`) is the local wherever it is in force: `eval.deprecations.items` is its field chain and `eval.deprecations.note(x)` a method call on it. Where no such binding is in force, including after its block ends, the spelling is the module path. A binding form the rewrite does not follow is refused with E_SHADOWING at the use.

typed-hole-unread-parameters.summary: A function whose body still holds a typed hole is not refused with E_UNUSED_CAPABILITY or warned with W_UNUSED_BINDING for a parameter it does not read, because the code that fills the hole may read it; once the hole is filled the checks apply again.

warning-display.summary: check, build, run and test print a warning in full unless its module is tracked by git and unmodified against HEAD; those are counted in one closing line (`warnings: 215 in 40 unmodified modules (...); `selka check --warnings` lists them`). `--warnings` and SELKA_WARNINGS=all print every warning, --diagnostics=json always carries every one, and a project that denies warnings prints all of them when it fails. build, run, run-project and test leave out the W_COPY_MOVE hints (not printed, not counted); check, lint, --warnings and --diagnostics=json show them.

test-cache-callbacks.summary: A test that invokes a callback through a local, a record field or a parameter is keyed and reused like any other: the receipt proof follows every function value the call tree creates. A test is refused a receipt (cache reason `live-effects: <finding and function>`) only for a Host capability, a host function, an extern func, a callback beside function_digest, or a callable test input.

admission-wait-variable.summary: scripts/build-slot.sh exports SELKA_ADMISSION_WAIT_S, the seconds (with milliseconds) a job waited from its request to its admission, to the command it runs, under the default and the scheduler backends.

core-store-disk-budget.summary: The per-user object store's collector counts allocated disk blocks against its 10 GiB cap instead of file lengths (a 96-byte checksum record holds a 4 KiB block), counts a hard-linked name once, retires the flat aliases of objects that have a shard name, and keeps its ledger in `.size-ledger-v4.sqlite3`.

limits.generic_calls: explicit arguments or complete inference from call inputs; ambiguous and unmaterialized phantom arguments require explicit specialization
limits.unit: Unit/() procedures; None is only an optional absence; main accepts int or Unit, optionally fails E, and explicit Result return types
limits.container_elements: managed list/dict elements: copyable values without must-handle obligations, owned resources, or capability grants
limits.noalloc: @noalloc is a build/run/test error when ownership-expanded Core may allocate; plain check does not compute this Core contract
limits.iteration: range(end/start,end), list/str/dict/fixed-array foreach and enumerate; fixed bounds and structural mutation checks
limits.native_runtime: the new core: Core IR to LLVM text, compiled with the pinned Zig toolchain's clang and linked with the core C runtime; amd64 Linux (SysV) only; foreign calls through scalar `extern func` with `--link FILE.c`
limits.workers: no host worker facility and no guest spawn syntax; parallelism is the task groups and parallel.map of docs/concurrency.md, on one thread pool per process
limits.floating_point: float literals, ordinary operators, signed int conversions; IEEE binary64; standard sqrt is the correctly rounded binary64 operation, decimal parsing (`parse_float`) is correctly rounded; sin, cos, exp, ln and the other transcendental functions are in `math` (docs/floating-point.md)
limits.callbacks: exact parameter types, named labels, mutation positions, return-origin contracts and failure contracts; no inferred effect ceilings, capturing closures or reference results
limits.semantic_reuse: ordinary checked bodies and concrete specializations replay across processes; symbolic templates keep abstract checking; unresolved nested or interned-identity references stay conservative; in-memory retention is bounded by one shared reuse.max_bytes budget and a zero budget disables reuse
limits.text_data: managed Unicode scalar strings and managed bytes; foreign calls take scalars only
limits.time_random: Unix wall clock and explicit entropy capabilities; deterministic noncryptographic SplitMix64
limits.managed_lists: owned growable storage; explicit independent copies; no resource or capability elements, stored borrowed interiors or host escape
limits.python: static fixed-width types, explicit const/mut bindings with lexical block scope and no active shadowing, checked ownership and explicit copies; indentation is the block syntax
limits.dictionaries: managed insertion order; homogeneous hashable keys (integers, bool, str, bytes, and records, enums, optional values and fixed arrays of those) and copyable values
limits.value_semantics: named managed moves use own except bare returns; const place bindings borrow, from declares borrowed results, and copy(value) creates independent storage. Prefix mut parameters and arguments preserve caller storage, including whole-value rebinding, fields and elements. class and Cell are rejected.
limits.sets: managed insertion order over hashable elements; `set()` needs an expected type; no frozenset, no augmented operators (`|=`); generic bodies key only by integer-bounded parameters, `str` or concrete hashable types; a module that declares its own function named `set` keeps it, and there the type spelling `set[T]` is unavailable while literals still work
limits.generators: Generator expressions report E_GENERATOR_REMOVED; use explicit collection loops or scalar folds, preserving early stopping for any/all. Suspended generator functions and stored generator values remain unsupported. Comprehensions and match-expression yield arms are also removed; use statement loops and match statements.
limits.native_tests: one native process per test; exported test_ functions returning bool or Result[bool, E]; positive deterministic receipts keyed by the test program's Core IR, settings, toolchain and outcome-relevant environment; a run with --link never reuses a receipt; --verify-facts separates its receipt keys from plain runs; directory runs share one worker budget (--jobs, SELKA_JOBS or CPUs)
limits.standard_library: forty-two embedded Selka modules, including lists, strings, csv, http, hashes, binary, process, cache_record, persistent_memo and durable
limits.memory: checked ownership, nonescaping borrows and direct destruction; no tracing collector. Identity graphs use pool handles. `with arena()` remains removed with a migration diagnostic

tuples.note: Wave1: tuple types, values, tuple returns and destructuring report E_TUPLE_REMOVED. Use nominal records with explicit fields; certain returns, consumers, swaps and sort keys carry migration fixes. enumerate, zip and dictionary items retain two-name loop bindings without materialized tuples.

destructuring-element-targets.note: Wave1: tuple destructuring and swaps report E_TUPLE_REMOVED. Certain swaps stage receiver/index/value evaluation into temporaries before ordinary assignments.

capability-effects.note: Wave1: source effect ceilings and inferred transitive effect facts were retired. effects(...) and noio report E_EFFECTS_REMOVED; capability arguments still carry authority explicitly.

derived-effect-ceilings.note: Wave1: derived effect ceilings, source effect clauses and their inferred interface metadata were retired. effects(...), noio and trailing noalloc report E_EFFECTS_REMOVED. A trailing body noalloc migrates to the surviving @noalloc Core allocation assertion; it is not an effect ceiling.

bounded-guest-callbacks.note: Wave1: callback effect ceilings report E_EFFECTS_REMOVED. Guest callbacks retain typed parameters, named labels, mutation positions, return-origin contracts and failure contracts; pass state explicitly to named functions.

python-print-and-output-effect.note: Wave1: inferred output-effect metadata was retired. Stream.print and out.print remain supported; authority is supplied by the Stream argument.

explicit-storage-tier.note: buffer/pool/list declarations, the allocator capability, references and slices, lexical borrows, legacy arena scopes and every standard module built on them. Managed collections and `with arena()` regions replace them.

c-backend.note: emit-c/emit-project-c, src/native.zig and the C-only runtime. QBE is the only native backend.

record-literals-without-new.note: merged into positional-and-named-record-constructors; the `new T { ... }` spelling it was named against left with the legacy brace syntax.

legacy-migration.note: selka migrate/migrate-project, src/migrate*.zig and their drivers. Their input was the brace dialect, which no longer exists.

legacy-syntax.note: the brace dialect: fn/let/let mut/struct/new, `T { … }` record literals, `::` qualification, `::<T>` turbofish, `cast<T>(x)`, `//` comments, `{ }` scope blocks, match expressions, `true`/`false`/`unit`, `else if` and `a..b` ranges. Indentation, `def`/`class`, `T(f=v)`, `alias.name`, `f[T](x)`, `T(x)`, `#` comments, `match`/`case`, `True`/`False`/`None`, `elif` and `range(a, b)` are the surface.

named-executable-laws.note: the sampled-law runner was a Python script (scripts/laws.py), never part of the compiler; it moved to experiments/guest-laws/ as an experiment. `selka test --cases` still runs one law case natively.

value-producing-matches.note: `match e { P => v }` had only a brace spelling and no Python one; a `match` statement whose arms return covers the same programs.

bounded-scalar-source-evaluation.note: the eval-project command, its step/frame/eval-byte budgets and its eval-report-v1 / evaluation-request documents. It executed a parameter-free entry in the compiler's own process; `selka run` builds the program natively and runs it instead.

bounded-vm-trace.note: vm_trace.Trace and the vm.Options.memory.trace hook. The ring of recent instructions it sampled was an interpreter artifact; a native guest reports a source-mapped call stack at its trap instead.

in-memory-host-replay.note: host_replay.Transcript and its recorded call comparison. It wrapped an interpreter provider registration, and a natively built guest calls its registered provider directly.

isolated-process-workers.note: scripts/workers.py and its typed-call-v1 job pool. Each job dispatched one guest call through invoke-project; nothing replaces it, and the language still has no spawn syntax.

memory-accounting-categories.note: selka-io --memory-report, --max-runtime-bytes, --max-vm-bytes and --max-host-bytes, and the runtime-memory-v1 split of VM bytes into guest backing and bookkeeping. There is no VM allocator to split; guest-memory-ceilings bounds a guest process instead.

mandatory-mutation-footprint-warning.note: `W_MUTATES_MISSING` and the reference-typed `class` exemption, with the `mutates(...)` clause and the opt-in `&` / `--mutation-markers` marker beside them. A parameter a function writes through is declared `mut name: T` and every argument bound to one is written `mut argument`; see the implemented `mut-parameters` entry.

unchecked-release-builds.note: `selka build --unchecked` (and `run`/`run-project`/`build --run --unchecked`, and the emitters' internal `--drop-safety-checks`) omitted the overflow, narrowing-cast and index-bounds guards and, with no ceiling, the frame record, so a would-be trap was undefined behaviour and optimization could change a program's result. Every build now keeps them (RELEASE-CHECKED-1), and `--unchecked` is refused as removed.

guest-test-gc-stress.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka test --gc-stress` ran tests under the tracing collector's stress mode. The flag remains refused; checked ownership is now the memory model.

nonmoving-tracing-gc.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): the single-threaded nonmoving tracing collector, `--gc-runtime` and `SELKA_RUNTIME=gc-v1`. Checked ownership now destroys managed objects directly when their owner ends.

managed-list-cycles.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): reclaiming cyclic managed graphs needed the tracing collector and legacy sharing. Value semantics cannot build a cycle; identity graphs use pool handles.

managed-arenas.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `with arena() as name:` regions and their escape checks (`E_ARENA_ESCAPE`). The spelling is rejected with `E_ARENA_REMOVED`; `selka fix` removes the block and unwraps escapes.

managed-class-records.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): legacy-sharing mode and its GC-managed `class` reference records, `--legacy-sharing` and the `value_semantics: false` opt-out. `class` and builtin `Cell` are rejected; use records for values and pool handles for identity.

rc-ownership-sites.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `--rc-runtime=sites` and `SELKA_RC_SITES`, the counting two-count RC runtime that charged ownership events to call sites. `selka build --stats` reports the new core's ownership plan.

ownership-explain.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka check --explain-ownership=OUT.jsonl`, which wrote the old bytecode ownership analysis. The flag is refused; `selka build --stats` reports the new core's ownership plan.

native-invocation.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka invoke` and its `native-invocation-v1` envelope, retired with host functions (S5-D5). Call the function from a `main` or a test.

module-compile.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka compile-module` and `link-modules`, the old back end's per-module QBE builds. `selka build` emits and caches one LLVM unit per module instead.

module-build.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): the module-by-module scheduler of `compile-module` children behind `build` and `run`. A debug build emits one LLVM unit per module and recompiles only units whose text changed.

module-check.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): module-by-module `selka check` from `compile-module` records. A project check checks the merged program with the semantic cache.

module-test.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): per-module test libraries built from `compile-module` records. `selka test` builds each test program with the new core and keys receipts on its Core IR.

guest-performance-benchmarks.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka test --bench*` with its baselines and policies, and `bench-promote` (S5-D6). Time a program with `selka run --timings` or an external benchmark harness.

host-application-guest-bounds.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): the host applications `schematic-svg`, `board-trial` and `selka-io` and the ceilings they chose for their guests (S5-D5).

signature-pure-outcome-replay.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka test --pure-skip`, which replayed a recorded outcome for a signature-pure test without running it (S5-D6).

test-diagnostics-json.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): `selka test --diagnostics=json` (S5-D6). `selka check --diagnostics=json` reports an entry that does not compile, `fix` fields included.

copied-block-byte-io.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): copied 256-byte blocks, an ABI of the retired `selka-io` byte runner host (S5-D5).

configurable-byte-io-budgets.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): the `selka-io` byte runner's input, output and execution budgets (S5-D5).

scoped-directory-and-endpoint-providers.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): the `selka-io` byte runner's `--allow-dir` and `--allow-endpoint` providers (S5-D5). `selka run --restrict --allow-read/--allow-write/--allow-endpoint` grants the same authority.

scoped-filesystem-metadata-and-listings.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): metadata and listings of the `selka-io` byte runner's scoped directory providers (S5-D5).

native-default-releasefast.note: Retired with the old back end in new-core stage S5 (2026-10): builds defaulted to QBE at ReleaseFast. A build is now a debug build, one LLVM unit per module, unless `--release` asks for the optimized whole-program build (`release-builds`).

direct-c-scalar-imports-qbe.note: merged into direct-c-scalar-imports when the QBE back end was retired (new-core stage S5, 2026-10); `extern def` calls work the same in every build.

fixed-array-negative-indices.note: Negative fixed-array positions are removed. Constant negative positions report E_NEGATIVE_INDEX_REMOVED with certain explicit-length fixes; computed negatives trap R_LIST_BOUNDS.

named-constraints.note: Named constraint bundles and op(...) requirements are removed with scalar domains. Use surviving built-in/field bounds and explicit callback parameters.

scalar-domains.note: Scalar domains, wrap/unwrap, type-owned operations and codecs are removed. Use ordinary records, invariants and free functions; records serialize as JSON objects.

sequence-repetition.note: Text, bytes and list multiplication/repetition is removed. Use strings.repeat, byte_builder.repeat, lists.filled or explicit loops.

list-membership.note: in/not in scans of lists and dictionary values are removed. Use lists.contains or explicit loops; dictionary-key, set, text and bytes membership remains.

structural-contracts.note: The former combined field/type-owned-operation feature is retired. Field requirements survive as field-requirements; op(...) requirements use explicit callback parameters.

expression-bodied-lambdas.note: Expression-bodied lambda callbacks report E_LAMBDA_REMOVED. Use named functions with explicit parameter and result types; selka fix extracts certain noncapturing callbacks in their original module.

conditional-expression.note: Conditional expressions report E_CONDITIONAL_EXPRESSION_REMOVED. Use if/else statements that assign an explicitly typed result or return from the selected branch, preserving operand order and short-circuit evaluation.

match-yield-expressions.note: Value-producing match expressions and yield arms report E_MATCH_EXPRESSION_REMOVED. Use a match statement whose cases assign a result or return; wildcard and payload patterns remain supported.

list-comprehensions.note: Both source-first and Python list comprehensions report E_COMPREHENSION_REMOVED. Build a typed list with explicit for/if statements and append, evaluating each produced value before appending it.

dict-and-set-comprehensions.note: Dictionary and set comprehensions report E_COMPREHENSION_REMOVED. Use typed collections with explicit nested for/if statements, dictionary assignment or set.add, preserving clause order.

generator-arguments.note: Generator expressions in calls report E_GENERATOR_REMOVED. Use explicit loops to collect values or fold a scalar; any/all folds must stop at the deciding value, including nested loops.

reference-counting.note: Reference counts, copy-on-write, retain/release/uniqueness IR operations and the counted block-header field were removed. Checked ownership is the sole memory model.

ownership-experimental-selectors.note: --experimental-zero-rc and --experimental-single-owner are rejected with exit status 2 and a message saying reference counting was removed. Plain commands use checked ownership.

list-snapshot.note: The hybrid ownership mode and list .snapshot() were removed. Transfer the owner, borrow it for a bounded lifetime, or use .copy() for independent storage.
